claim: Judge Mehta's Sept 2, 2025 remedies opinion in US v. Google does not ban Google's default search payments to Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla, only bars exclusive distribution deals.
stance_target: whether the Google TAC payment to Apple is barred or preserved
scope_conditions: US v. Google search antitrust case, District Court for D.C., Sept 2025
quoted_support: The judge has allowed these default payments to continue based on his expectation that generative AI companies will exert competitive pressure on Google Search in the future, and out of concern that Google's search distributors would suffer without default payments from the monopolist, while barring Google from striking exclusive distribution deals.
numbers: tens of billions of dollars per year

claim: Mehta retains authority to revisit a payment ban if the ordered remedies fail to restore competition, but the timeline for reopening is undefined given pending appeals.
stance_target: remedy is repricing/renegotiation risk rather than a resolved binary
quoted_support: Judge Mehta notes that his court is prepared to revisit the idea of a default payment ban (or other payment-related solutions, perhaps) if competition is not substantially restored through the other remedies. The timeline for revisiting the payment ban decision is uncertain given likely appeals in the case and to-be-determined conditions for reopening the payments question.

claim: Google's scale advantage in search is extreme: ~90% of total queries and 95% of mobile queries, versus 6% and 1% for Bing respectively; 13 months of Google user data equals 17 years of Bing user data.
stance_target: magnitude of switching-cost floor for alternative bidders
scope_conditions: cited from the liability opinion / trial record
quoted_support: Google receives about 90% of total queries (95% on mobile) compared to 6% for Bing (1% on mobile), its next closest competitor. The user-side click and query data that Google collects in 13 months is equivalent to 17 years' worth of Bing user data.

claim: Data-sharing remedies (web index and user-side query data) were narrowed by the court from periodic to one-time (index) or 'at least twice' (user data) disclosure, undermining their competitive utility according to KGI analysis.
stance_target: remedy is largely toothless / status quo preserved for Google
scope_conditions: US v. Google remedies opinion, data-sharing provisions
quoted_support: Judge Mehta changed the frequency of user-side data sharing from "periodic basis" to "at least twice," with a to-be-defined cap on the total number of data transfers per competitor.

claim: 93% of search queries in a sampled query log were seen only by Google, versus about 5% seen only by Bing, illustrating the long-tail data moat that alternative bidders would have to overcome to bid comparably for default placement.
stance_target: alternative bidders (Bing, OpenAI, Perplexity) could easily pay comparable sums for non-exclusive default placement
scope_conditions: Plaintiffs' expert query log sample, US v. Google trial
quoted_support: The Plaintiffs' expert examined a query log sample and found that 93% of the queries were seen only by Google, whereas about 5% were seen only by Bing.

claim: KGI's follow-on commentary 'Pay for Half' proposes capping (not banning) Google's default-search payments, opening at least half the market to rivals including AI entrants while preserving revenue for distribution partners like Apple.
scope_conditions: proposed remedy design discussed during pending appeal, published July 2026
quoted_support: In Pay for Half, KGI's Alissa Cooper joins leading economists and competition experts in showing how the court can reasonably cap those payments rather than ban them, opening at least half of the market to rivals, including emerging AI-powered entrants, while preserving revenue for distribution partners.
